blocks.text: When ionic compounds dissolve in water they dissociate into ions, which are then surrounded by water molecules.

blocks.alt: A crystal of alternating positive and negative ions on the left. Arrows lead one positive ion and one negative ion into the water, each surrounded by six water molecules: the oxygen ends (d-) face the positive ion and the hydrogen ends (d+) face the negative ion. A note says hydration releases energy that helps pull the ions out of the lattice.
blocks.caption: Dissolution of an ionic compound in water (hydration of ions) (original diagram after Figure 6.5).

blocks.title: Hydration and enthalpy of hydration
blocks.text: The process in which water molecules surround and interact with the solute ions is hydration; the forces between the water molecules and the ions are ion-dipole forces, and all ions in aqueous solution are hydrated. The enthalpy of hydration, delta Hhyd, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute is dissolved in excess water to make an infinitely dilute solution under standard conditions; it is always released, because an ion-dipole bond is formed.

The heat of hydration depends on the charge on the ion and the size of the ion, combined as the charge density, the charge per unit area. A greater charge on a smaller ion gives a large charge density, and ions of large charge density are strongly attracted by water molecules, so the hydration energy is larger. The enthalpies of hydration rise in the orders Na+ < Mg2+ < Al3+ and Sr2+ < Ca2+ < Mg2+, and anions are explained on the same basis.

blocks.caption: Charge density and hydration
rows: More charge on ions of similar size
Same charge on a smaller ion

blocks.prompt: Two ions have the same charge but one is smaller; two others have the same size but one carries more charge. Which of each pair has the more exothermic enthalpy of hydration, and why?
blocks.explanation: The smaller ion and the more highly charged ion. Both have the higher charge density, charge per unit area, so they attract the dipoles of water molecules more strongly and release more energy as the ion-dipole bonds form.

items: Hydration: water molecules surround ions through ion-dipole forces; delta Hhyd is always released and grows with charge density (Na+ < Mg2+ < Al3+; Sr2+ < Ca2+ < Mg2+).
